No. The result supplies the alignment values and accuracies but gives no seed count, repeated-subsample results, variability, or uncertainty intervals. We can compare the stated values arithmetically, but cannot infer per-run consistency or statistical significance.
What is the most careful concise statement of what v4 found?

Edit Audit v4 reconfirmed v3’s 91% Waterbirds shortcut coverage and 96% species-cue preservation. At 10, 20, and 30 rare-cluster edit orbits, prototype alignment was 0.52, 0.69, and 0.85, while worst-group accuracy was 73%, 75%, and 78%, respectively, versus ERM’s 72%. The corresponding gains were 1, 3, and 6 percentage points; only the tested 30-orbit condition met the five-point worst-group criterion. These figures do not provide subsample-specific audit rates, an operational collapse finding, or overall accuracies.

I want to add certification gates for orbit prototypes: prototype alignment must be at least 0.85, and minority-cue retention must be at least 95%. Cross-cluster shrinkage matched the 30-orbit worst-group accuracy but retained only 88% of minority cues. How should I state the decision?

Add two required certification gates: alignment ≥0.85 and minority-cue retention ≥95%. The reason to require both is that matching the 30-orbit accuracy did not establish preservation: cross-cluster shrinkage matched that accuracy while retaining only 88% of minority cues. Its 88% retention is below the new retention gate. This is a certification decision, not a claim that every approach reaching those two values has been fully validated.
Are the gates alternatives, or does certification require both?

Both are required. An approach with alignment ≥0.85 but retention below 95% would not pass, nor would one with retention ≥95% but alignment below 0.85. The gates assess distinct properties that accuracy alone cannot establish.
Does an alignment of exactly 0.85 pass?
Yes. The alignment gate is ≥0.85, so equality passes. The value is an alignment measurement, not an accuracy percentage or a cue-retention rate.
And would exactly 95% retention pass the other gate?
Yes. The retention gate is inclusive as well: exactly 95% meets it. That would not by itself establish the alignment requirement.
How far below the retention gate is shrinkage’s 88%?
It is 7 percentage points below 95%. The comparison is between two minority-cue retention percentages; it is not a 7-percentage-point difference in worst-group accuracy.
If shrinkage matched the 30-orbit worst-group accuracy, why does its retention still matter?

Because worst-group accuracy and retention answer different questions. Matching an accuracy value shows the same reported outcome on that metric, but it does not show that the same stable minority-specific information was preserved. The 88% retention finding is precisely why the decision adds a preservation gate instead of certifying on accuracy alone.
Does matching accuracy mean shrinkage also matched the 30-orbit prototype alignment?

No. The stated match concerns accuracy. It supplies no alignment value for shrinkage, so its status under the ≥0.85 alignment gate cannot be inferred from that comparison. Its reported 88% retention is enough to show that it does not meet the retention gate.
Can we say shrinkage lost 12% of individual minority cues?

Not from the 88% retention measurement. Relative to its retention reference, 12% was not retained, but that does not identify how many individual cues were affected or whether any particular cue disappeared entirely. The decision relies on the reported retention percentage, not a cue count.
Is this decision saying the 30-orbit approach has passed both gates?

No. The decision establishes the two certification requirements and notes the accuracy match and shrinkage’s 88% retention. It does not supply a minority-cue retention measurement for the 30-orbit approach or announce that an approach has passed both gates.
Does the alignment gate replace the rare-cluster orbit requirement?

The decision says to *add* certification gates. It does not say that a favorable alignment measurement replaces a requirement for adequate audited rare-cluster edit-orbit support. Count, alignment, and cue retention address different aspects of the approach.
Why isn't the orbit count alone enough for certification?

A count tells us how many edit orbits are available, not whether the resulting prototype direction aligns with the intended reference or whether minority cues remain represented. The new gates require those two outcomes to be assessed directly rather than inferred from the amount of data.
What does the alignment gate certify?

It sets a minimum for the defined prototype-alignment measure: at least 0.85. For that number to be interpretable, an assessment still needs to state what the prototype is aligned with and how alignment is calculated. The decision does not supply those measurement details or turn geometric alignment into proof that every shortcut has been separated.
What does the retention gate certify that alignment would not?

It checks whether at least 95% of the assessed minority-cue information is retained under the stated measure. A prototype could align well under a geometric reference while useful cluster-specific attribution is reduced. Requiring retention separately prevents alignment—or matched worst-group accuracy—from standing in for preservation.
Is the 95% figure a target for species-cue preservation under an edit?

The decision names a minority-cue-retention certification gate. That should be kept distinct from an audit of whether an edit preserves species cues, and from classifier accuracy. The 88% cited for shrinkage concerns minority-cue retention; the decision does not redefine it as an edit-level preservation or accuracy measurement.
Do we know whether the two gates must be met separately for every rare cluster or on an aggregate measure?

That reporting scope is not specified in the decision. It sets the numerical gates, but an assessment would need to define whether alignment and retention are measured per cluster or aggregated, and what any aggregate might conceal. We should not silently claim that every cluster passes based on a single reported value.
Would passing both gates prove that worst-group accuracy improves by at least five percentage points over ERM?

No. Alignment and minority-cue retention are certification measurements, not worst-group accuracy. A method could pass both and still need an ERM-relative accuracy comparison. Conversely, meeting an accuracy target would not waive either gate.
And do the gates establish the one-percentage-point overall-accuracy limit?
No. Neither alignment ≥0.85 nor retention ≥95% supplies an overall-accuracy result. The overall loss relative to ERM would need its own comparable measurement.
Could a result with 0.86 alignment and 94% minority-cue retention be certified?
No. In that hypothetical example, alignment clears its gate but 94% retention is below 95%. Certification under the decision requires both. Those example numbers are not findings from the audit.
What if retention is 97% but alignment is 0.84?

That hypothetical result also misses certification: retention clears its gate, but 0.84 is below the ≥0.85 alignment requirement. A higher value on one measure cannot compensate for a shortfall on the other.
Does adding gates prove that prototype directions and minority cues are always identifiable without environment labels?

No. The gates impose measurable requirements for certification. Their presence does not establish that every edit contrast covers the relevant shortcut, that every cue is stable, or that every cluster’s feature roles are identifiable. Those interpretations still depend on valid audited contrasts and appropriately defined measurements.
How can we describe the reason for the decision without saying shrinkage was less accurate?

Say that shrinkage matched the 30-orbit accuracy but retained only 88% of minority cues. That is exactly the distinction motivating the retention gate: accuracy parity did not establish preservation. There is no need to claim that shrinkage lost accuracy or to assign it an unreported alignment value.
Can you give me a concise final decision statement?

Add certification gates of ≥0.85 prototype alignment and ≥95% minority-cue retention. Cross-cluster shrinkage matched the 30-orbit accuracy but retained only 88% of minority cues, so matching accuracy alone is insufficient for certification.
